power.what: Power on site: how well solar, wind and geothermal power would do at each place, with the Moon and Mars beside it.
power.rough_estimate: A rough estimate by our own rule. It is not a measurement or an engineering study.
rules_in_words: Panel yield, rule of thumb: kWh a day from each kilowatt of panels = sunlight on level ground (kWh per square metre per day) x 0.75. A panel's kilowatt rating assumes 1 kW per square metre of sunlight; 0.75 allows for heat, dirt, snow, wiring and inverter losses. Panels tilted toward the Sun do better at high latitude (a low Sun hits a level panel at a glancing angle); that is not counted here.
Solar class 'good': yearly mean sunlight on level ground of at least 4.5 kWh per square metre per day (about 1,640 kWh per square metre a year).

Solar class 'fair': from 3.0 up to 4.5 kWh per square metre per day; 'poor' below 3.0. These cut values are our own: sunny deserts (5.5 to 7) read good, central Europe (about 3) fair to poor, the high Arctic (about 2) poor.
A month counts as having no sunlight (polar night) when NASA POWER gives exactly 0.0 for it; a month the service leaves blank is unknown (null), not dark.

Sunlight above the air at the distance of Earth and the Moon from the Sun: 1,361 watts per square metre (NASA NSSDCA Earth and Moon fact sheets, saved in this project). At the Moon's south pole a panel standing upright and facing a Sun on the horizon receives all of it, because there is no air.

Air mass at Sun height h (degrees), the thickness of air the sunlight crosses relative to a Sun overhead, by the cited 1989 study, Applied Optics 28(22), 4735-4738: AM = 1 / (sin h + 0.50572 x (h + 6.07995)^-1.6364). Sea level; the place's height is not counted.

Direct beam on a panel facing the Sun through clear air, by the cited 1976 study, Applied Solar Energy (Addison-Wesley), as quoted by PVEducation: beam = 1,361 x 0.7^(AM^0.678) watts per square metre. 0.7 is the share passed by one air mass of typical clear air; the exponent 0.678 allows for air that is not uniform.
The power is worked out at each lunar Sun ceiling (the limit_deg of each region in grazing_cells.json) and at half its height, because the Sun spends much of the low-Sun hours below the ceiling.

A place's clear-sky share in its best ten-day periods = mean of (1 - cloud percent / 100) over the months of the ten-day periods listed in grazing_cells.json under targets.<region>.top_bins, weighted by the low-Sun hours of each period. Cloud percent is cloud_pct of cloud_cells.json (monthly mean over all hours, CERES SYN1deg). The low-Sun power under the place's typical sky = clear-sky figure x that share. Null where the region has no best periods at the place or the cloud is unknown.
Air density at sea level in the International Standard Atmosphere: 1.225 kilograms per cubic metre.

Air density at height z metres (International Standard Atmosphere, lower 11 km): 1.225 x (1 - 0.0065 x z / 288.15)^4.2559. z is the mean height of the model grid box the 50 m wind is given for (as the service names it in each answer); where the service gives no height, sea-level density is used and the height is null. Cold polar air is denser than the standard atmosphere (about 10 % at -15 C), which would raise the figure; that is not counted.

Factor for the usual spread of wind speeds: if speeds follow a Rayleigh distribution the mean of the speed cubed is 6 / pi = 1.91 times the mean speed cubed, which is how the standard 50 m wind classes were tied to mean speeds.

Power in the wind at 50 m = 0.5 x air density x 1.91 x (yearly mean speed)^3, in watts per square metre of rotor area: the power the moving air carries, not what a turbine delivers (a turbine takes at most 59 %, in practice 35 to 45 %). The yearly mean speed is the plain mean of the 12 monthly means of NASA POWER's WS50M.

Wind power classes 1 to 7 at 50 m (US Department of Energy and NREL, the cited 1986 study, Wind Energy Resource Atlas of the United States; at sea level these match mean speeds of 5.6, 6.4, 7.0, 7.5, 8.0 and 8.8 m/s): class 1 below 200 W per square metre, 2 from 200, 3 from 300, 4 from 400, 5 from 500, 6 from 600, 7 from 800. The bands are from the published table as we know it; no copy was saved tonight.
Wind class 'good': class 4 or higher (at least 400 watts per square metre at 50 m).
Wind class 'fair': classes 2 and 3 (200 up to 400); 'poor': class 1 (below 200).
Geothermal class 'good': a working geothermal power plant (WRI Global Power Plant Database, primary fuel geothermal) lies within 50 km ...
... or a volcano that erupted since 1990 lies within 30 km.
'Erupted since 1990': the Smithsonian list of volcanoes gives a last eruption year of 1990 or later, or its list of eruptions holds a confirmed eruption that started or ended in 1990 or later.
Geothermal class 'fair': a working geothermal plant within 150 km, or any volcano of the Holocene (the last 11,700 years) within 100 km ...
... 'poor' otherwise.
Distances are along the ground (great circle) from the area or square centre, on a sphere of mean Earth radius 6,371 km.
NASA POWER is asked one request at a time, at least 2 seconds apart.
On a refusal (429) or a server fault (5xx) we back off at least a minute.
On a dropped network we wait 20, 40, 60 ... seconds (at most 300) and try again.

panel_factor.unit: kWh per kW of panels per kWh per m2

density_with_height.unit: lapse K per m, sea-level K, exponent

wind_power_rule.unit: W per m2 of rotor area

power.classes: each part has a class in plain words (good, fair, poor; null where its inputs are unknown) and the figures behind it
power.null_rule: Unknown is null, never 0. A real 0.0 (a month of polar night) stays 0.0.

what_it_is.solar: Sunlight on level ground: NASA POWER ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN, all solar energy (direct plus diffuse) reaching a level surface per day under the real sky, monthly mean over the service's years, for the 1 degree box that holds the place (CERES SYN1deg). Yearly mean = plain mean of the 12 months. Panel yield and class by the rules above.
what_it_is.low_sun: Clear-air power on a panel facing a Sun at each lunar Sun ceiling and at half of it, from the air mass of the cited 1989 study and the direct-beam formula of the cited 1976 study, then times the place's clear-sky share in its best low-Sun ten-day periods.
what_it_is.wind: Mean wind speed 50 m above the ground: NASA POWER WS50M (POWER from the MERRA-2 reanalysis), monthly mean over all hours, at the MERRA-2 grid point nearest the place (0.5 by 0.625 degrees). Power in the wind and class by the rules above. ws10m_ms_year is the 10 m speed of the power-extra group (WS10M), given for comparison.
what_it_is.geothermal: A rule-of-thumb class from what is steadily there: working geothermal power plants (WRI Global Power Plant Database) and volcanoes of the last 11,700 years and those that erupted since 1990 (Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program). The figures behind it: nearest plant with name, size and distance; plants and megawatts within 150 km; nearest volcano erupted since 1990; nearest Holocene volcano.

what_it_is_not.solar: Not what a tilted or tracking panel would make, not a measurement at the place, and not the light of the low-Sun hours only. A coarse box of about 111 km by 20 to 55 km at these latitudes.
what_it_is_not.low_sun: Not measured; diffuse light from the sky is left out; real polar air (haze, ice crystals, aerosol) varies; cloud is a monthly mean over all hours and a box about 111 km tall, not over the low-Sun hours. This is a textbook clear-air estimate: real polar air and haze vary from day to day, so a real panel can get less or somewhat more; it shows that Earth's low Sun delivers only a fraction of the power the same low Sun gives a panel on the Moon, where no air stands in the way.
what_it_is_not.wind: A coarse grid mean (a box of about 55 km by 20 to 35 km here), not a measurement at the place: local hills, coasts, valleys, ice slopes (katabatic winds) and icing of the blades change it greatly. Not what a turbine would deliver.
what_it_is_not.geothermal: Nobody has drilled or measured heat here: it only says that hot rock is likely to lie near the surface. A place far from volcanoes can still have useful warm ground (deep basins, hot springs) and a place by a volcano can be unusable. No open worldwide map of geothermal potential could be fetched without a login tonight. The plant list stops in about 2021 and misses some plants.

moon_and_mars.unit: power at the same wind speed, Mars / Earth (= air density ratio)
moon_and_mars.mars_wind_speeds: 2-7 m/s (summer), 5-10 m/s (fall), 17-30 m/s (dust storm) (Viking Lander sites)
moon_and_mars.how: Air densities as the two NASA NSSDCA fact sheets give them (Mars 'Surface density ~0.016 +/- 0.006 kg/m3', Earth 'Surface density 1.217 kg/m3'; saved in data/raw/mars_climate/factsheets/). Power in the wind is proportional to air density at a given speed, so the ratio of the densities is the ratio of the power. Cross-check: density = pressure x molar mass / (gas constant x temperature), with the site pressures of mars_sites.json, the fact sheet's mean molecular weight 43.49 and average temperature 214 K.
moon_and_mars.source: NASA NSSDCA Mars and Earth Fact Sheets (saved); data/derived/mars_sites.json

moon_and_mars.what: geothermal on the Moon and Mars

notes_from_the_sanity_look: Sunlight comes in 1 degree boxes. Yungay in the Atacama (square m_-24.25_-70.25) lies at the east edge of a box that reaches about 80 km out over the Pacific and its coastal cloud deck, so it reads 5.96 kWh per m2 per day; the next box inland (square m_-24.25_-69.75) reads 7.21, close to the highest in the file (7.38, on the Altiplano).

The highest 50 m winds (yearly means of 17 to 19 m/s) are on the coastal slopes of East Antarctica, where the MERRA-2 model's katabatic winds run strong; the 10 m wind of the same model is nearly as high there. Model values, not checked against stations; blades there would also face extreme gusts and icing.
High ground has thin air: on the Tibetan Plateau (grid height about 5 km) the same mean wind carries about 40 % less power than at sea level, a small step toward Mars, where it carries about 1 %.
Geothermal 'poor' does not mean no warm ground: Tibet has a working plant (Yangbajain) 400 km from our square and many hot springs without volcanoes, which this rule does not see.

steady.place_point: the area centre (lat and lon in grazing_cells.json); an area is about 11 km across, so any point of it can be up to about 8 km nearer or farther than the figures say
steady.what_this_is: For every place: what volcanoes and people steadily do there (not the risk of a rare event), with the useful side of each (young volcanic ground; help within reach), and a small-tremor class (the catalogue's verdict where it can see small tremors, our rough estimate where it cannot). Read beside the light ranking, not part of it.
steady.rule_of_thumb: A rough estimate by our own rule. It is not a measurement.
rules_in_plain_words: A rough estimate by our own rule. It is not a measurement.

volcanic, 'steady volcanic effects likely': a volcano that erupted in 3 or more separate years since 1990, or at any time since 2015, lies within 30 km of the place's centre. What it means for the work: gas and volcanic haze that can corrode and fog instruments and optics; fine ash and abrasive dust on the ground and in the air; warm or steaming ground that upsets temperature readings; small volcanic tremors; closures of the area when it erupts.

volcanic, 'volcanic effects come and go': a volcano that erupted since 1990 lies within 100 km. What it means for the work: gas and volcanic haze that can corrode and fog instruments and optics; fine ash and abrasive dust on the ground and in the air; warm or steaming ground that upsets temperature readings; small volcanic tremors; closures of the area when it erupts.

volcanic, 'young volcanic ground (useful side, yes or no)': yes when a Holocene volcano (active in the last ~11,700 years, any date) lies within 50 km and the rock map (data/derived/rock_frozen_cells.json or mars_rock_frozen.json, when present) calls the place's rock volcanic; no when there is no such volcano within 50 km or the rock map says the rock is not volcanic; null when a volcano is that close but the rock map gives no class. Fresh lava and ash are a good stand-in for the basalt soil of the Moon's dark plains and of Mars.

human, 'steady human disturbance likely': a listed settlement of 1,000 or more people lies within 5 km, or a main road or railway within 2 km, or an airfield with scheduled flights within 10 km. What it means for the work: vibration from vehicles and aircraft; radio noise; dust raised by traffic; artificial light; tracks and litter in camera views.

human, 'human disturbance possible': a listed settlement of any size lies within 25 km, or a main road or railway within 10 km, or an airfield of any kind within 10 km. What it means for the work: vibration from vehicles and aircraft; radio noise; dust raised by traffic; artificial light; tracks and litter in camera views.
human, 'undisturbed as far as our lists show': otherwise.

human, 'help within reach (useful side, yes or no)': yes when a listed settlement of 1,000 or more lies within 50 km or an airfield with scheduled flights within 100 km (power, shelter, rescue); no otherwise.
small tremors, 'small tremors likely': a volcano that erupted since 1990 lies within 50 km, or at least 5 earthquakes of magnitude 5 or more were catalogued within 200 km since 1990.

small tremors, 'small tremors possible': a Holocene volcano of any date lies within 100 km, or 1 to 4 earthquakes of magnitude 5 or more within 200 km since 1990, or glacier ice covers 10% or more of the area's land (moving ice makes small quakes).

volcanic.class: one of the three classes of the rules
volcanic.effects: the fixed list of what a steady or recurring volcanic presence does to field work; the same words for every place of the class, not observed at the place; empty for 'none expected'
volcanic.decided_by: the volcano that set the class (the nearest one meeting the class's test), or null
volcanic.nearest_erupted_since_1990: the nearest volcano with a confirmed eruption in progress in 1990 or later, any distance: name, GVP number, km, the number of separate calendar years since 1990 with an eruption in progress, the last such year, and whether the list says it is still going on
volcanic.nearest_holocene: the nearest volcano of the Holocene list, any date (it can be the same volcano)
volcanic.young_volcanic_ground: true, false or null by the rule; the useful side, kept apart from the class
volcanic.rock_map_volcanic: the rock map's own yes/no (null when it gives none), copied from the rock file
volcanic.is_not: Not a hazard map, not an eruption forecast. A volcano is one listed point (summit or field centre); a fissure system or field can reach well beyond it, and gas or ash can drift much farther than 100 km downwind. 'Years erupting' counts calendar years in which the list has a confirmed eruption in progress: an eruption with no end year counts its start year only; uncertain and discredited eruptions are left out; lava lakes and steady degassing between listed eruptions are not counted (a volcano can steam and smell for decades between them).

human.class: one of the three classes of the rules
human.why: which of the class's tests held, in words
human.effects: the fixed list of what steady human presence does to field work; empty when undisturbed
human.nearest_settlement: nearest listed settlement (GeoNames cities1000), its population (null when the list gives none) and km
human.nearest_settlement_1000_or_more: nearest listed settlement whose listed population is 1,000 or more
human.population_within_25km: sum of the listed populations of the settlements whose point lies within 25 km: 0 when none is listed, null when some are listed but none has a figure, a lower bound when only some lack one
human.nearest_main_road_or_railway: the nearest Natural Earth 1:10m road or railway (ferry routes left out), with its class, type, name and km; km null and none_within_km 1000 when there is none that close
human.nearest_airfield: nearest runway airfield of any size (OurAirports small, medium or large airport, gravel and ice strips included; heliports, seaplane bases and closed fields left out, as in data/derived/access_cells.json), with km
human.nearest_airfield_with_scheduled_flights: the same, among airfields the table flags as having scheduled service
human.help_within_reach: true or false by the rule; the useful side, kept apart from the class
human.is_not: Not a population map and not a noise or light measurement. A straight line, not a travel distance. GeoNames cities1000 lists places of more than 1,000 people and seats of local government, so camps, stations, mines and hamlets are missing; Natural Earth holds main roads and railways only, so a missing road is not proof of no road (tracks, winter roads, mine roads are mostly absent); an airfield's traffic is not known, only that it exists.

small_tremors.class: the catalogue's verdict from the tremors file where it has one, else our estimate
small_tremors.catalogue_verdict: the verdict of data/derived/tremors_cells.json (or mars_tremors.json), null if the file or the place is missing
small_tremors.our_estimate: our rule's class, worked out for every place so it can be compared where the catalogue sees
small_tremors.m5_quakes_200km_since_1990: earthquakes of magnitude 5 or more within 200 km, 1990-2025, from the hazards file (null if the file is missing)
small_tremors.glacier_ice_share: share of the area's land mapped as snow and ice (ESA WorldCover in the north; the south's ice-sheet share), from the landcover files; null for the Mars squares
small_tremors.is_not: Not a count and not a measurement of small tremors: a guess from what usually makes them (active volcanoes, a seismically busy region, moving glaciers). Small tremors can occur where it says unlikely, and need not occur where it says likely.

steady.null_rule: unknown is null, never 0; a count of 0 means the list holds none within the radius
steady.distance: great circle on a sphere of radius 6371.0 km (haversine); against the real ellipsoid within about 0.5 percent
steady.roads_accuracy: points added along every road and railway so none is more than 1.5 km from the next; the distance to the nearest point overstates the distance to the line by at most 0.75 km. Natural Earth 1:10m lines are themselves generalised (often a kilometre or more off the real road)
steady.search: grid indexes (1 degree cells; 0.5 degree for road and rail points); every kept point is decided by its great-circle distance; nearest searches widen until they find a point (roads and railways: up to 1000 km)

tremors.what: Small tremors near each place: catalogued events of magnitude 1 to under 5, how often, how steadily, how large, and whether the catalogue can see small tremors there at all.
tremors.magnitude_range: 1.0 up to (not including) 5.0, any magnitude type, as the catalogue gives it

rule_of_thumb.words: our rule of thumb, not an engineering standard: 'steady small tremors' when catalogued events fell within 100 km in at least 12 of the 16 years and at a rate of at least 5 a year; 'occasional small tremors' when at least one fell within 100 km but not steadily (in 1 to 11 of the years, or under 5 a year; 1 to 3 years is usually a single swarm); 'none recorded' when the catalogue records small tremors here and none was catalogued within 100 km; 'cannot tell' when the catalogue cannot see small tremors here, and also when it sees only tremors above some magnitude between 2.5 and 3.5 and none was catalogued within 100 km (an empty circle then says nothing about smaller ones).
rule_of_thumb.status_words: The detection floor is the 10th percentile of the magnitudes of all catalogued events from 1 to under 5 within 500 km over the 16 years (null if fewer than 30 events). 'small tremors are recorded here' when the floor is at or below 2.5; 'only tremors of magnitude M and above are recorded here' when it is above 2.5 and at most 3.5; 'small tremors cannot be seen in this catalogue here' when it is above 3.5 or there are too few events to tell. A floor at or below 2.5 counts only if the catalogue also lists at least one event under that magnitude within 200 km of the place (field floor_check); otherwise the low floor is borrowed from a better-watched network farther away, as western Alaska seen from Chukotka or Texas seen from Coahuila, and the place is read as 'cannot be seen'. Where small tremors cannot be seen the counts are null, never 0: no record is not the same as no tremors.

fields.small_per_year_50km: mean number a year of catalogued events of magnitude 1 to under 5 within 50 km of the place centre, 2010-2025; null when the catalogue cannot see small tremors here
fields.years_with_events_100km: in how many of the 16 years at least one such event was catalogued within 100 km (the 'consistent' part: 14 of 16 is steady, 1 of 16 is one swarm); null when the catalogue cannot see small tremors here
fields.median_magnitude_100km: median magnitude of those events within 100 km (null if none)
fields.largest_small_magnitude_100km: largest magnitude among them, always under 5 (null if none)
fields.nearest_small_event_km: distance to the nearest catalogued event of magnitude 1 to under 5, searched out to 500 km (null if none that close)
fields.share_not_earthquake_100km: share of the events within 100 km that the catalogue types as something other than an earthquake (quarry blast, explosion, ice quake and so on); these shake instruments too and are counted
fields.events_500km_for_floor: how many catalogued events of magnitude 1 to under 5 lie within 500 km: the sample the floor is read from
fields.detection_floor: estimated smallest magnitude the catalogue reliably records in this region: the 10th percentile of the magnitudes within 500 km (null if fewer than 30 events)
fields.floor_check: 'passed' or 'failed: ...' where the floor was at or below the 'recorded' line: whether at least one event under it is catalogued within 200 km; a failed check turns the status to 'cannot be seen' (null where the check does not apply)
fields.catalogued_anyway_100km: only where small tremors cannot be seen: the events the catalogue still lists within 100 km (count, years, smallest magnitude), mostly magnitude 4 and up; a sign of activity and a lower bound, not a rate of small tremors (null otherwise)
fields.verdict: plain verdict for instruments, by the rule of thumb in meta.rule_of_thumb

tremors.what_it_is_not: A count of catalogued events, not a measurement of ground motion at the place; not a hazard map; a seismometer on site is the only real test. The catalogue lists only what nearby seismometers detected, so its reach differs by region: in Alaska it sees magnitude 1 to 2, in the remote Arctic, Siberia and Antarctica almost nothing under 4. The networks also grew during the 16 years (north of 55 N the catalogue lists about 1.6 times as many events of magnitude 1 to 5 a year in 2017-2025 as in 2010-2015; in some places, such as the Kobuk valley, several times as many), so early years undercount and 'years with events' leans low. Distances are from the place centre.
tremors.edge_note: Events were fetched poleward of 55 degrees. For areas between 59 and about 59.5 N the 500 km circle reaches a little south of 55 N, so the floor there is read from slightly fewer events.
tremors.grid_index: events in 1-degree bins; each search reads only the bins that can reach the circle, then measures great-circle distance
